sources.headline: EU chief lays out vision for new Canada partnership at Montreal summit
sources.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has laid out her vision for what an "associate membership" status for Canada to the EU would look like as officials gather in Montreal to discuss closer ties. It is "a partnership that comes close to membership than anything we have done before," she said on Thursday's remarks at the two-day Canada-EU summit.She added it is a type of relationship that would be open "only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together."It includes close alignment on governance and policies, and partnering in research and innovation. For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this year's meeting in the Canadian city. Thursday and Friday's summit is being closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.Von der Leyen first proposed "opening the door" to Canada last month for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship. Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement last month. While there is broad support for closer ties, the concept of "associate membership" is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada, he said."Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.Despite some opposition, von der Leyen has continued to use the term has not addressed the disagreement over the term. Later on Thursday, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days. Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months. But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic. Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties."The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit. Polls show the majority of Canadians support forging closer ties to Europe, external, though the Conservative opposition in Canada has criticised the effort as a distraction from other issues, like the high cost of living. "No one's mortgage or grocery bill will come down," said Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre in a statement, adding that Canada already has a free trade pact with the EU. Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer. US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway. Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme. It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.On Thursday, Canada released its new National Security Strategy, the first in two decades, which underlines supporting security and stability in Europe as a priority.As for what this new relationship status will be called, Carney has said the "nomenclature" does not matter. "What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

sources.headline: EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
sources.text: The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between member states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he ​interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.“The good news is it doesn’t matter about ⁠specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will ​make to the lives ​of Canadians.”A previous draft statement ​had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, ​including an acknowledgment that ‌defining the ​term would take ​another year.

Published: 3:43am, 30 Oct 2026

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Thursday the EU and Canada continue to explore Canada becoming the union’s first “associate member”, a term so divisive among member countries that it does not appear in a joint declaration.

The European Union and Canada aim to deepen cooperation on AI, climate, energy and security, von der Leyen said in a speech at a Canada-EU summit in Montreal.

The ‌associate member term, which Germany and several other EU countries oppose, has no legal meaning.

“Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession,” von der Leyen said. “We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before.”

“We can work on everything, from AI and climate to energy or security,” she said.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen speaks before the 21st EU-Canada summit in Montreal on Thursday. Photo: AFP

Canadian and EU leaders, however, dropped the idea of associate EU membership from their joint declaration, seen by Reuters, agreeing instead to an “ever closer association”.

The declaration, which officials plan to make public on Friday, said work to define the Canada-EU relationship would continue until another summit next year.

Deeper ties to ⁠Europe are part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. ‌

Still, Canada’s efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue.

Von der Leyen first floated associate membership for Canada six weeks ago, prompting a rebuke from countries that argued they could not agree to a concept that had ‌no legal status and had not been fleshed out, diplomats said.

Three EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity, said they were surprised von der Leyen ⁠continued to use the “associate member” term, since ⁠the declaration deliberately excluded it.

Speaking later at the summit, European Council President Antonio Costa said the idea of associate membership for Canada was “audacious”, but that he shared von der Leyen’s ambition.

A previous draft statement had included at least ‌two references to Canada as an associate member, including an acknowledgement that defining the term would take another year.

US President Donald Trump (right) meets with Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney in the Oval Office in October 2025. Photo: Reuters

Carney said the term for Canada’s new relationship with the EU is insignificant. “This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The ‌name doesn’t matter,” ‌he told reporters.

“What matters is that the complementarities of our two jurisdictions strengthen our sovereignty, strengthens Europe’s sovereignty, various strategic autonomies, critical minerals, energy, other aspects, AI,” Carney said.

Canada and ‌the EU were both trying to find an effective response to the geopolitical threats Trump has posed, said Mark Manger, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs at the University ⁠of Toronto.

“Canada and the EU both are now in this position where the most important ally they relied upon is suddenly not behaving like an ally any more,” he said.

⁠Manger said Canada and the EU have an enormous opportunity to expand their relationship, but that it would take time to address regulatory inconsistencies, build new undersea cables linking Canada to Europe and secure common supply chains, some of the objectives mentioned in the joint declaration.

The declaration also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian ‌liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and enabling ‌young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.

Von der Leyen called for deeper cooperation between the EU and Canada on Arctic security.

“When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbours and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the European Union and Canada,” she said.

“We have to act and change our strategic posture and, together with like-minded partners like Canada, stand up for these values.”

sources.headline: Canada-EU summit: What do both sides want, and what’s at stake?
sources.text: Canada is set to host a summit with the European Union to bolster bilateral strategic and economic ties as its relations with its southern neighbour, the United States, are in sharp decline.The summit is scheduled for October 29 to 30 in Canada’s French-speaking city of Montreal, and is expected to focus on closer cooperation on trade, technology, defence, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, research and financial services.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Canada, US and tit-for-tat tariffs: How will they impact their economies?list 2 of 4Canada’s Carney welcomes EU’s associated membership proposallist 3 of 4Why does Canada want to join the Europe-led JEF military partnership?list 4 of 4Why is Canada’s PM Carney not ruling out a possible war with the USend of listIn September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the move.What is the summit, and why is it happening now?This will be the 21st Canada-EU summit and is expected to build on the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force in 2017. It eliminates duties on up to 99 percent of all imported goods between the two sides, according to the European Council.“In Montreal, we will take our partnership to the next level by launching our ‘Alliance for the Future’ to deepen our political, economic and institutional ties even further,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, who will be attending the summit along with Carney and von der Leyen. They are expected to issue a joint statement.The deepening Canada-EU alignment seems fuelled by US President Donald Trump’s policies, which imposed hefty tariffs on both Canadian and European exports to the US and pushed Canada to look for ways to reduce its economic dependence on the US. Before Trump’s tariffs whipsawed relations, Canada sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to the US.In August, trade talks between Ottawa and Washington, DC, broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.US President Donald Trump has unleashed tariffs on Canada, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has hit back with retaliatory tariffs on the US [File: Evelyn Hockstein/Pool/AFP]What do Canada and Europe want from each other?Both sides are seeking opportunities that will open more options beyond the world’s largest economy.“The opportunity is clear. The EU brings market power, research depth, and manufacturing strength. Canada brings abundant energy, critical minerals, world-class capabilities in space, artificial intelligence (AI), and quantum, and one of the world’s strongest banking systems,” Carney’s office said in a statement.The summit will give the two sides a chance to turn these “complementary strengths into concrete benefits for our peoples,” the statement added.Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a think tank in Ottawa, Canada, sees benefits and challenges.“These fields could be beneficial for both sides, and we are likely to see specific announcements during the summit on these sectors,” she told Al Jazeera.“The main challenge is how quickly the political momentum can turn into specific deals and projects to deliver specific economic results,” she added.The EU describes Canada as “the only non-European country” taking part in Security Action for Europe (SAFE), the EU’s 150 billion-euro ($167bn) loan programme that supports and expedites defence procurement by EU member states.The EU concluded its agreement with Canada, allowing it to participate under SAFE, in February, and it gives Canadian firms preferential access and treatment in defence procurements financed by the SAFE Instrument.Could Canada become an associate member of the EU?Last month, von der Leyen proposed that Canada could become the EU’s first associate member, suggesting a deeper relationship spanning trade, technology, defence and economic security.Carney later welcomed the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.However, the term “associate member” does not currently exist in EU treaties or its standard enlargement framework, according to the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), a Brussels-based think tank.“The term does not actually matter; what is important is the practical deepening of the relationship and the actual results, no matter what the final term is,” Nadjibulla said.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has suggested that Canada could become the EU’s first ‘associate member’ [File: Patrick Kovarik/AFP]Is it an anti-American alliance?“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said in her address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg last month, which Carney attended, making him the first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address.Nadjibulla agrees.“I do not see that as an anti-US coalition. It is rather about diversification of economic and defence partnerships and building resilience for Canada. It is a continuation of Canadian Prime Minister Carney’s policies to create opportunities. A deeper alliance with Europe is essential to this agenda,” she said.“President Trump will likely not appreciate this, but it is about Canada having more choices in an unpredictable world,” she added.Bob Rae, former premier of Ontario and Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025, told Al Jazeera that “President Trump does not control our policy. We have been having long and productive relations with the Europeans for hundreds of years, but Trump chose to treat Canada in a way that does not respect our sovereignty”.He added that “engaging in conversations with the EU is perfectly normal and is not directed at the US”.Trump has threatened the European Union with new tariffs over its proposal to make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member”, suggesting the move could be considered hostile to the US.“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters in Charlotte, North Carolina, in September.Trump dismissed the prospect of Canada joining the EU as “laughable” and called the US’s northern neighbour a “terrible trade partner”.

Canada and EU drop associate membership plan in bid to deepen ties 
 Canada and the European Union will pursue closer ties but have dropped a proposal for associate EU membership, according to a joint declaration ahead of Thursday’s summit in Montreal. Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US, despite warnings from Donald Trump.   
 
 
 
 
Issued on: 29/10/2026 - 01:56Modified: 29/10/2026 - 07:30
    3 min Reading time   
  Share     
 
  By:  
 
  FRANCE 24       
 
     
 Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on September 17, 2026. © Pascal Bastien, AP    
 
Canada and the European Union (EU) agreed to "ever closer association" but dropped the contentious idea of associate EU membership in a joint declaration seen by Reuters ahead of a Montreal summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney starting on Thursday. 
The declaration, which officials plan to make public on Friday, said work to define the Canada-EU relationship would continue until another summit next year. 
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's suggestion of associate membership six weeks ago had been a divisive issue in negotiations among EU countries on the summit declaration, with Germany leading a group that argued they could not sign up to a concept that had no legal status and had not been fleshed out, diplomats said. 
Deeper ties to Europe are an important part of Carney's strategy to reduce Canada’s economic and security reliance on America since US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. Still, Canada's efforts to draw closer to the EU risk angering Trump as trade talks between Canada and the US continue. 
There is no precedent or legal definition for an EU “associate member”.

Trump previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable” and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act,” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”. 
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week is the launch of further formal negotiations that will take another year. 
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.” 
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an associate member, including an acknowledgement that defining the term would take another year. 
The statement includes a joint initiative to improve international connectivity between Europe, Canada and Asia through "new subsea cable infrastructure". It also proposes conducting a joint feasibility study on Canadian liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and enabling young Canadians and Europeans to work across the Atlantic.

Julian Karaguesian, a former adviser at Canada’s Finance Ministry, described the summit as “a bit of a show”. “Canada’s effort to be closer friends with the EU is very ill-defined,” he said, adding that increased collaboration with the EU would not necessarily address Carney’s drive to diversify the country's relationships. Canada ships nearly 70% of its exports to the US while the EU accounts for about 9% of Canada’s total trade. 
Carney's office declined to comment. 
'Highly provocative' statement 
The statement says European and Canadian leaders pledge to reaffirm their commitment to a rules-based international order and that they “deeply regret” the sanctions the US imposed on the Netherlands-based International Criminal Court. 
“All that talk of multilateralism and support for international law is basically like sticking a finger into President Trump’s eye,” said Barry Appleton, an international trade lawyer and fellow at the Balsillie School of International Affairs in Waterloo, Ontario. 
Read moreFrance, Germany seek new EU rapid response tool against trade threats 
Appleton said Canada and the EU agreeing to work closely on economic security measures might anger the US. He added that the statement commits Canada to making its AI and digital rules work alongside Europe’s, when Washington considers EU-style digital regulation a trade barrier. 
“This is a highly provocative statement from the EU and Canada,” Appleton said. 
The White House said in response to a request for comment that US and Canadian trade officials are talking. 
EU officials said at a briefing Tuesday that the summit was a “historic milestone”, saying it was about renewing their commitment to Canada and shaping an ambitious new chapter in the partnership. They said all member states support the closest possible relationship with Canada. 
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

sources.headline: EU removes mention of ‘associate membership’ from Canada declaration
sources.text:
Published on
28 October 2026 - 15:59 GMT+1
The EU has dropped any mention of associate membership from the latest draft of the joint declaration due to be adopted at the end of the EU-Canada summit in Montreal on Thursday and Friday.
The proposal, introduced at Germany’s insistence in a revised text circulated to member states on Wednesday, has been replaced by a commitment to “ever closer association” between the EU and Canada, but short of full membership itself.
The office of European Council President António Costa has spent recent hours in intense talks with several member states, above all Germany, which objected to the term in the political declaration.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea in her State of the Union address to the European Parliament last month, inviting Canada to become the first EU associate member.
An earlier draft was put to member states on Tuesday under the silent procedure, under which a text is deemed adopted unless a country explicitly objects. Germany, France, Italy and Greece all raised issues with it.
Germany has been the most vocal opponent of the term. Chancellor Friedrich Merz had previously proposed a similar status for Ukraine as a way to give Kyiv security guarantees before it fully joins the bloc.
For Berlin, the priority is to define what closer cooperation with Ottawa means in practice, rather than shoehorn the package into a term that is absent from the treaties and could carry significant legal implications.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has favoured the phrase “alliance for the future”, saying he wanted to focus on the substance of the agreement and that the terminology was for the EU to settle.
The latest version of the text has been submitted again for silent procedure, meaning it will be adopted unless EU countries object to it later this afternoon.
